extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature and drama; playwrights and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for composing and evaluating dramatic works (especially tragedy and comedy), focusing on the relationship between plot and character, idealisation/generalisation, the ludicrous, and the requirements of unity, development, and ethical portraiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as first necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is artistically the first necessity of the drama: the drama is a poetical representation of a complete and typical action, whose lines converge on a determined end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot 'evolves itself out of human emotion and human will, in such a manner that action and character are each in turn the outcome of the other.' The plot should not be merely a series of external incidents but should be the medium through which character is discerned and tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must not overpower character
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot does not overpower character; it is the very medium through which character is discerned, the touchstone by which its powers are tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where a 'supreme necessity' guides events, the tragic action should be a struggle of moral forces so that character remains visible and operative in the unfolding of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and completeness of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama should represent a complete and typical action with a beginning, middle, and end whose lines converge on a determined end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greek drama exemplified this unity; modern/romantic drama sometimes enlarges scope, but the ideal dramatic structure still requires unity so action and character cohere into a typical, determinate whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility of character with plot/tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be fitted harmoniously into the framework of a particular plot; the predetermined end of traditional legends can constrain ethical portraiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatists working with consecrated legends (Greek) were limited: 'the end was a thing given; and in the drama the end cannot but dominate the structure of the whole—incidents and character alike.' This can weaken denouement if the plot tradition is inflexible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to invent within subject-matter limits
rubrics_metrics.description: While poets had freedom to delineate character, their invention was restricted by choice of subject matter and audience expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dramatist might exhibit the same person under inconsistent types across works, but when fitting persons into a particular plot the poet's ethical portraiture is hampered. Audiences familiar with heroic legends were 'not prepared for bold surprises.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Character development (character in process)
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern drama often exhibits character in growth — to be shown each step in the process from germ of deed in the mind to its ripening into action and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We desire to be present 'at the determining moment of a man's career, to watch the dawning of a passion, the shaping of a purpose, and to pursue the deed to its final accomplishment.' Examples: Macbeth as a complete instance of development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between subjective introspection and dramatic action
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive reflective or introspective analysis of character can mar dramatic effect by producing characters lacking the energy of will to carry action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goethe's reflective emotional characters often result in 'dramatic biographies' rather than historical dramas; the introspective habit yields dramatic lyrics but may fail to produce effective drama if will/agency are weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation and the representation of the universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry idealises — represents objects in their permanent and essential aspects, enlarging particulars into the human and universal; tragedy and comedy both embody types rather than mere individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idealisation does not mean flawless virtue; a particular quality must be thrown into relief while preserving the equipoise of character that constitutes a typical human being. The idealised character should answer to the 'true idea' without destroying balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic characters as embodiments of universal principles
rubrics_metrics.description: In Greek tragedy heroes embody great principles (Religion, State, Family) and pursue objective ends rooted in social ideals; characters gain universal meaning and validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic characters are 'concrete embodiment of these forces' and are free from inward discord and self-contradiction; their aims are objective and appeal beyond their own age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's focus on the follies and the particular aspect of life
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy concerns itself with the follies, foibles, flaws and imperfections of humanity, exhibiting negative or limiting aspects of life rather than the rounded, complete action of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy 'withdraws its attention from the graver issues which concern the end of conduct' and often embodies a dominant characteristic so that 'the single attribute becomes the man.' It can give artistic expression to types that serious art cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's tendency to abstraction and caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Because comedy often isolates a single dominant characteristic to embody a type, it risks running to caricature and 'framed on lines of impossible simplicity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic method abstracts and exaggerates one trait (covetousness, misanthropy, etc.), producing a one-sided view of character; details are accentuated differently from tragedy and frequently serve the general effect rather than moral completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between genuine comedy and personal satire/invective
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine comedy represents the universal and is distinct from personal satire (lampooning, invective), which represents the particular and aims at abasement of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle excludes personal satire and 'galling caricature' from true comedy; coarse abusive language and malicious lampooning (old Attic political comedy) are different in kind from the generalising comedy he prefers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of typified names and masks to generalise character in comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy can use characteristic names and masks (e.g., the Boor, the Parasite) to signal types and promote generalisation of human follies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Middle and New Comedy adopt names suggesting qualities so the type is immediately recognised; titles like 'the Boxer' or 'the Fault-finder' communicate typical human traits in service of universalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The ludicrous: defect without pain or destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: The ludicrous is 'a defect or ugliness, which is not painful or destructive' — ugliness that does not cause pain and provokes laughter by painless incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's account omits malice: the pleasure of the ludicrous arises from the perception of incongruity and a transition or change of mood (unexpected resemblance or unlikeness). Laughter may ally with malice or sympathy but is not essentially malicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity plus transition required for the ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity alone is not always ludicrous; to be comic it requires a transition (change of mood) resulting in discovery of unexpected resemblance or unlikeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pleasure of the ludicrous arises from the 'shock of surprise at a painless incongruity' and involves a blending of contrasted feelings; good comic effect depends on timing of that transition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of certain permanent human imperfections in art
rubrics_metrics.description: Art must accept certain flaws as permanent features of common humanity; comedy works with these imperfections by making them objects of mirth rather than hatred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What counts as accidental or abnormal will vary by period and art form, but some imperfections will always be seen as normal and thus legitimate material for comic treatment; shown as nugatory, they can contribute to the beauty of the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance individual particulars with universal function in character-drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: A character universalised for drama may still be 'ugly' when considered alone yet contribute to the beauty and meaning of the whole dramatic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual details are not suppressed; both tragedy and comedy aim at the type rather than mere individual, and particulars serve the universal representation (e.g., Aristophanes' use of historical names as types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale, pacing, and scope affect character depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The period embraced by action and the scope of representation influence how much character can expand and undergo essential changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greek conventions (short plays, four dramas in a day) limited scope; romantic and modern drama often extend temporal span (sometimes approaching a trilogy) allowing fuller growth and development of characters across stages of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulation of moral probability and consistency in comic plots
rubrics_metrics.description: As comedy evolved (Middle/New Comedy), action gained strength and consistency so that 'moral probability' replaces arbitrary sequences and typical follies are woven into a credible plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change produces closer study of real life, finer delineation of motive, and an action with beginning, middle, and end; typified follies are integrated into plots that appeal to universal human sentiment.
